items.title: How a Robot Tests an Action Before It Moves
items.summary:
How can a robot test an action without moving? NVIDIA's Ming-Yu Liu explains how a world model predicts the outcome first.

Cosmos 3 learns three abilities together: forward dynamics (what happens after an action), inverse dynamics (which action caused a change) and policy (what the robot should do next). The results in the paper show that each one helps the others. The payoff is a closed-loop simulator. Instead of setting up a thousand kitchens, developers can check a robot policy in simulation before trying it for real.

Full interview: https://youtu.be/L6tLBApQN-g

Learn more about Cosmos: https://nvda.ws/4cJoY1S

items.title: How Physical AI Learns Across Language, Video and Action — Ming-Yu Liu
items.summary:
The car making a left turn at the start of this episode was never filmed. Cosmos 3 generated it. Ming-Yu Liu, who leads the Cosmos research at NVIDIA, explains how one model can describe a video, generate one, and produce robot actions.

He walks Tim through the architecture. A vision language model reasons one token at a time; its weights then initialise a bidirectional diffusion generator for video, audio and action, and a shared temporal position scheme lines up signals that run at different rates. Ming-Yu treats "world model" as a set of tools, not one definition: forward dynamics, inverse dynamics and policy, trained together under a capacity limit so that each helps the others. He also explains why plentiful first-person human video carries over to robots, which have far less data of their own, and why a Cosmos model post-trained on the DROID dataset is a good starting point for pick-and-place policies.

The most practical thread is testing. A neural simulator does not need accurate success rates. It only needs to rank policy A above policy B the way the real world would, so a team can narrow down which checkpoints deserve a real trial. Cosmos Dreams applies that closed-loop idea to driving and robotics, and Ming-Yu argues that humanoids around children and pets make safety matter even more than it does for cars. The conversation ends on the Super, Nano and Edge sizes (Edge targets Jetson Thor, Orin and DGX Spark) and where to find the open weights, code and data.

This episode is a paid partnership with NVIDIA.

Learn more about Cosmos: https://nvda.ws/4cJoY1S
Explore Cosmos Lab: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/cosmos-lab/cosmos3/

items.title: Spec-Driven Development
items.summary:
For AI coding agents, accurately specifying your intent is the whole ballgame! Spec-Driven Development: Engineering with intent teaches you how to close the gap between what you mean and what your agents actually build.

In this session, we’ll ask these questions:
- Why does vibe coding break down as projects grow?
- How can teams turn vague ideas into precise AI-ready intent?
- What makes a specification different from a detailed prompt?
- How does spec-driven development reduce context debt?
- How can teams align with coding agents before implementation begins?
- What should every effective specification contain?
- How can specs enforce architectural constraints and coding standards?
- How do teams write thorough specs without slowing development?
- How can AI help developers uncover missing requirements?
- How do specs improve the review of AI-generated code?
- Why do specifications become stale, and how can teams prevent it?
- How should teams handle gaps between a spec and its implementation?
- Can living specifications replace outdated project documentation?
- How does spec-driven development support teams using multiple AI agents?
- How can teams choose the right spec-driven development tools and workflows?

items.title: A day in the life of a Cryogenic Systems Engineer
items.summary:
In August 2026, IBM successfully connected and cooled two cryogenic modules into a single operating environment: 
https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog/modular-cryogenics
 
The achievement validates a fundamental design principle behind the IBM Quantum roadmap: Quantum computers of the future should be built as modular systems.
 
Instead of housing processors inside isolated cryostats, our architecture creates connected cryogenic cells that can be linked together while maintaining the ultra-cold temperatures required for quantum computation.
 
In this video, IBM Quantum Cryogenic Assembly Engineer Allie Lindler answers some of our most frequently asked questions about this new modular approach to housing and cooling quantum processors, including what it takes to achieve and maintain scalable, ultracold temperatures as a cryogenics specialist.

items.title: The Reason Most Always-On AI Agents Die in Two Weeks (with Dilani Kahawala)
items.summary:
#aiagents #aiassistant #aistartup 

In Episode #1027, Dr. Dilani Kahawala (Co-Founder and CEO of Anna) joins @JonKrohnLearns explain what it takes to build an always-on AI assistant that busy parents will trust with their inboxes. Anna watches the email, school apps, WhatsApp messages and calendars flowing into a family's life and surfaces what matters, over text and voice, with barely any app to speak of. Dilani came to it by way of a Harvard physics PhD, McKinsey, and a decade of product leadership at Etsy, Meta and Atlassian, and says she has had to throw away most of what that decade taught her about how products get built. In this episode, she lays out the three hardest problems in building Anna, why the eval loop is the heart of the product, how a long-running agent differs from a turn-based one, and the brutal unit economics of consumer AI.

items.title: Inside quantum optimization research
items.summary:
Optimization is often cited as one of quantum computing’s most promising applications. Businesses and researchers are constantly searching for better routes, schedules, allocations, and ways to allocate limited resources, meaning that a computational advantage for quantum optimization methods could deliver enormous value. Yet despite years of research, fundamental questions remain: Which optimization problems are best suited to quantum computers? And how will we know when quantum methods have truly surpassed their classical counterparts? 

 

In this episode of the Coherence Times, we’re joined by IBM’s Stefan Wörner and Stephanie Riedmüller of the Zuse Institute to explore the promise and limitations of quantum optimization. Together, they discuss the search for new quantum algorithms, the importance of benchmarking and community-driven research, and what it will take for quantum computers to deliver practical advantages for real-world optimization problems.  

Learn more about quantum computing and explore the IBM Quantum Platform → https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com

items.title: Why Voice AI Still Needs a Screen | Pavan Muddireddy
items.summary:
Ordering food by voice alone is harder than it sounds: without a menu in front of you, you have to hold every item in your head while you decide. Pavankumar Reddy Muddireddy, who leads audio research at Mistral AI, uses that example to explain why he expects voice to sit on top of a screen rather than replace it. The screen lets you take in information quickly and gives you proof that the system did what it said.
